decision_maker: Corporate Director: Resources
content:

Contract Standing Order 17.2(a) and, where applicable, Contract
Standing Order 17.2(e), and the direct award to Server Consultancy,
acting as an authorised partner of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, for
End-of-Life Extended Support for the Council’s HPE data
storage system.
 

2.    
To approve expenditure of £165,000 excluding VAT for the
period 01 September 2026 to 30 June 2027. This represents the full
financial commitment required to maintain manufacturer-level
extended support for a critical end-of-life system.

support arrangement, ensuring no gap in critical support coverage
for a system that is beyond its supported life and currently
experiencing active component failure. Early approval secures
continuity of service, maintains access to the only viable source
of specialist manufacturer-level support, and supports a controlled
transition to the longer-term replacement solution.

decision_maker: Corporate Director: Growth and Environment
purpose:
Approval has been granted for redevelopment of
the Council owned Leigham Court Road car park site, off Leigham
Court Road, for residential use. This is part of a wider
comprehensive development comprising three adjoining sites
including the car park. This report seeks approval to undertake a
statutory consultation on the revocation of parking controls in the
Leigham Court Road off-street car park and the amendment of the
supporting Traffic Management Order (TMO) to facilitate the
development.
content:
1.             
To authorise officers to commence statutory
consultation under the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 and in
accordance with the Local Authorities’ Traffic Orders
(Procedure) (England and Wales) Regulations 1996 on the revocation
of the Leigham Court Road car park from the Lambeth (Off-Street
Parking Places) (Amendment No. 1 ) Order 2023 as described in this
report with statutory consultation likely to take place in
September/October 2026 (closure date dependent on result of the
statutory consultation as outlined in recommendation 2). Cost of
statutory consultation likely to be in the region of
£2,000.

 

2.             
To agree to the
making of the relevant Traffic Management Order
(TMO) under sections 35 and 124 and Part IV of Schedule 9 of the
Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984, subject to no material objections
resulting from the statutory consultation process, but that if any
material objections are received they are considered by the
Assistant Director of Parking, Network Management and Fleet by way
of a separate written report before a decision is
reached.
 
3.             
To delegate to the Assistant Director for Parking,
Network Management and Fleet authority to decide whether or not to
hold a public inquiry pursuant to Regulation 9 of the Local
Authorities Traffic Orders (Procedure) (England and Wales)
Regulations 1996 as referred to at Section 4 of this
report.
 
4.             
To note the Equality Impact Assessment prepared for
the purposes of this report attached at Appendix B

decision_maker: Corporate Director: Growth and Environment
purpose:
The Council currently operates 500 Electric
Vehicle Charge Points (EVCPs) in-house under an “own and
operate” model, where the assets are owned, operated and
maintained by the Council. The Clenergy EV back-office platform is
used to operate the EVCPs via a contract with SEE Services
Ltd.

There is scope to reduce operating costs by contracting directly
with Clenergy, removing management fees and reducing transaction
and data fees in order to deliver savings of between £55,000
- £88,000 per annum with further savings expected as the EVCP
network expands. This will enable the Council to make significant
cost savings each year, without impacting service quality.
content:
To award a direct
contract to Clenergy EV via the G-Cloud
Framework for the provision of electric vehicle charging point
back-office management and data services for a period of two years,
commencing on 8 August 2026 and expiring on 7 August 2028, with an
estimated contract value of £321,000.

decision_maker: Cabinet Member for Economy, Cost of Living and Empowered Communities
purpose:
A cabinet member decision is required to
‘formally consider the Vauxhall One BID proposal and instruct
the Returning Officer to hold the necessary fifth term
ballot’.

The council is statutorily bound to consider the BID proposal and
hold a ballot on the BIDs behalf unless the proposal conflicts any
formally adopted and published policy by the council, or it is
likely to have a significantly disproportionate financial burden on
any person or class of persons.

This decision follows statutory timelines that must be followed
throughout the programme.
content:
To authorise a fourth term ballot
for Vauxhall One Business Improvement District (BID) due to take
place in November 2026. 
 


To request that the Chief Executive
as Returning Officer and “Ballot Holder” holds a ballot
for Vauxhall One BID at an estimated cost of
£2,500. 
 


To delegate authority to the
Director of Legal and Governance to complete the necessary legal
agreements required for the operation of the Vauxhall One BID levy,
the ballot and service agreements and any other matters required
for the Vauxhall One BID proposals in consultation with the
appropriate officers.  
 


To delegate authority to the
Corporate Director of Resources or Director of Finance to complete
the ballot papers to vote on behalf of the council in favour of the
BID proposal with regards to Council owned properties in the BID
area.
topline: The Cabinet Member for Economy, Cost of Living and Empowered Communities has decided to authorize a fourth term ballot for Vauxhall One Business Improvement District (BID) in November 2026.

decision_maker: Assistant Director - Parking, Network Management and Fleet
content:
1.   
To have due regard to the representations received during the
statutory objection period and officer responses thereto
(Appendix C) for the school street schemes currently in operation
at Iqra VA primary school, Glenbrook Primary School, Harris Academy
Clapham; La Retraite Roman Catholic
Girls' School; and an extension of the School Street at Henry
Cavendish primary school (Streatham) as detailed in the plans in
appendix B.  
 

To note the Equalities Impact
Assessment in Appendix D. 

 

To authorise the making of an order
which gives permanent effect to the experimental order for the
school street schemes shown in Appendix B under the provisions of
Sections 124 and Schedule 1 and Part IV of Schedule 9 of the Road
Traffic Regulation Act (RTRA) 1984 and Regulations 23 and 24 of the
Local Authorities’ Traffic Orders (Procedure) (England and
Wales) Regulations 1996 by September 2026.  

 

Subject to the schemes being made
permanent, to approve the continuation of the policy that enables
owners of vehicles to apply for a digital exemption permit allowing
vehicle access to the school street zones for: 

 

residents with vehicles registered
to an address within the school street, as shown in Appendix
A, 


owners of vehicles nominated by
residents living at addresses within the School Street Zones that
display a Blue Badge,   


owners of vehicles
nominated by the school (on behalf of pupils, parents, and staff)
displaying a Blue Badge. 
 


To agree that the responses received
to the experimental traffic order, including objections to the
proposals, do not warrant the holding of a public inquiry pursuant
to Regulation 9 of the Local Authorities Traffic Orders (Procedure)
(England and Wales) Regulations 1996. 

 

That subject to the existing
experimental schemes being made permanent to authorise officers to
carry out both informal public engagement and subsequent statutory
consultation on the reduction of the school street arrangement in
Rodenhurst Road as detailed in Appendix
I under the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 and in accordance with
the Local Authorities Traffic Orders (Procedure) (England and
Wales) Regulations 1996. This statutory consultation is expected to
take place in autumn 2026.  

 

That subject to due consideration
being given to the consultation mentioned at 6 above, to agree to
the implementation of proposed amendments to the School Street
arrangements on Rodenhurst Road as
detailed in Appendix I, and to making the relevant permanent
Traffic Management Orders (TMOs) under sections 6, 124 and Schedule
1 and Part IV of Schedule 9 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act
1984, subject to no material objections resulting from the
statutory consultation process, but that if any material objections
are received they are considered by the Assistant Director of
Parking, Network Management and Fleet by way of a separate written
report before a decision is reached as to whether to make the Order
as advertised (or not) or modify the proposals and, where required,
re?advertise and on whether a public inquiry pursuant to Regulation
9 of the Local Authorities Traffic Orders (Procedure) (England and
Wales) Regulations 1996 should be held before making such an
order. 

 

To approve the spending of
approximately £3,000 to implement the permanent
order.
topline: The Assistant Director of Parking, Network Management and Fleet has decided to make permanent the school street schemes at various schools and extend the scheme at Henry Cavendish primary school in Streatham.

Director of Regeneration, Growth and Capital Investment be

Indemnity Agreement (CPOIA) with Metropolitan Housing Trust (MHT)

delivery of pay by phone paid parking technology in the borough.
The ability to pay for parking by phone provides service users with
a customer friendly and simple way of paying for parking, whilst
reducing Council costs.

In October 2024 a Business Case was approved to pursue an open
tender process to procure a new contract, with the intention of
maintaining the current service levels whilst realising savings
from the new contract. In November 2025 the procurement was
abandoned through advice from Procurement and Legal services.

The purpose of this report is to seek approval for the Council to
join the National Parking Platform (NPP), a Department for
Transport (DfT) supported digital platform that enables driver to
find, access and pay for parking through multiple providers using a
single, open system.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
The Medium Term Financial Strategy Report will
provide an update on the economic outlook, pressures, risk areas
and set out the revenue funding deficit for 2027-31 together with
proposals to close the funding gap
content:
The item was also introduced by Councillor
Zvikomborero Chihoro, Cabinet Member for Finance and Community
Wealth Building. The following key points were highlighted:

The report updated the
Council’s Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) following a
review of assumptions made in March against the latest available
information.
The main changes related to council
tax assumptions within the Government funding settlement and timing
differences relating to school deficit balances.
It was noted that the MTFS assumed
council tax increases for planning purposes, but that any decision
on council tax would be taken by Full Council.
The budget gap for 2027/28 had
reduced from £37m to £19m, while the cumulative gap
across the three years to 2029/30 remained £93m.
The importance of invest-to-save and
income generation measures was emphasised.

Anne Crane, on behalf of the Transport and
Planning Sub-Committees of the Norwood Forum, addressed Cabinet and
raised the following points:

The proposed investment in electric
vehicle charging infrastructure was welcomed, particularly where
this was funded through Section 106 and grant funding.
It was requested that charging
infrastructure be distributed fairly across the borough, including
in areas with fewer public transport options.
The importance of designing charging
facilities to meet the needs of disabled people was highlighted,
including avoiding cables across pavements.
Consideration was requested of safe
arrangements for residents to charge vehicles from their own homes
and for secure charging of electric bikes.

Cabinet Members responded that:

Accessibility would be a key
consideration in the rollout of electric vehicle charging
infrastructure, with further engagement with disabled
people’s organisations and user groups welcomed to inform
design and delivery.
The administration was committed to
expanding electric vehicle charging as quickly as feasible, while
recognising financial constraints and the need for fair
distribution across the borough, including in the south.
The safety of electric bike
batteries and charging arrangements was highlighted, including
risks affecting gig economy workers and residents in houses in
multiple occupation.

Councillors Claire Holland and Bryn Scott
addressed Cabinet and raised the following points:

Concerns were raised regarding the
forecast £11m overspend and the need to understand this
within the wider context of structural underfunding, historic
borrowing and rising demand.
It was stated that the previous
administration had balanced the budget and consulted widely, while
concern was raised regarding the new administration’s
transparency and plan to address the financial position.
Questions were raised regarding the
assumptions around council tax, the basis of the financial review,
its remit, timeline, public involvement and opposition
involvement.
Concern was raised regarding the
absence of a timeline for savings proposals and clarification was
sought on the 35 new capital projects, including their funding and
impact on existing commitments.
Questions were raised regarding the
financial impact of pausing the Central Hill dementia service
relocation and how this would be addressed.

Councillor Chris Nicholson addressed Cabinet
and noted:

The importance of collaboration was
emphasised, while concern was raised that mitigation decisions had
already been taken without sufficient collaboration.
Concerns were raised regarding the
future years of the MTFS, including the 2027/28 gap, the potential
impact of the current year overspend, and larger gaps in later
years.
It was stated that campaigning for
additional government funding would be important, but that the
Council also needed to plan for how gaps would be managed.

Cabinet Members made the following
comments:

It was that stated previous
decisions, including Homes for Lambeth, empty council properties
and historic repairs decisions, had created significant financial
pressures, and that prioritising repairs would help reduce
longer-term disrepair costs.
It was stated that council tax
assumptions in the MTFS represented prudent financial planning and
did not constitute a decision to raise council tax.
Concerns were raised regarding the
financial impact of the Lambeth Children’s Homes Redress
Scheme, and why the £175m cost had fallen to the Council
rather than national government, given the wider systemic failures
involved.
The value of community assets and
services was highlighted, including the social value of dementia
care, community spaces and culturally important assets.
The pause to the Central Hill
dementia service relocation created a cost pressure, but
alternative options were being explored to maintain appropriate
dementia care provision while balancing the budget.
It was stated that financial
decisions should consider long-term social value and wellbeing, not
only short-term financial savings.

In response to questions and comments,
officers advised that:

The Lambeth Children’s Homes
Redress Scheme had been funded locally in the absence of a national
scheme, as had similar schemes in other authorities, although the
administration could lobby central government for recompense.
The independent financial review
would use the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy
(CIPFA) Financial Management Code as its foundation, covering 17
standards across six broad principles.
The review would be supplemented by
consideration of workforce management costs, project delivery
costs, legal and governance costs, financial control, housing
costs, procurement and contracts.
Relevant previous independent
reviews, including work relating to Homes for Lambeth, would be
brought together to provide a comprehensive assessment.
A full update on the capital
programme, including details of capital projects and borrowing,
would be provided through the Quarter 1 report in September.
The Council’s accounts,
including the group accounts incorporating Homes for Lambeth, were
due to be published, with the public inspection period to begin the
following day.

RESOLVED:

To note the budget gap of
£19.096m for 2027/28 as set out in Table 4 arising from the
Council’s updated Medium Term Financial Strategy.
To note the cumulative budget gap
for 2027/28 to 2029/30 of £93.217m as set out in Table
4.
To consider the risks discussed
within this report and to agree to receive an updated budget risk
register as part of the 2027/28 budget report.
To confirm the Council’s
commitment to delivering the existing agreed revenue savings
planned for 2027/28 (£31.132m), 2028/29 (£21.515m) and
2029/30 (£0.546m), a total of £53.193m.
To note the reserve position and the
need to ensure it continued to be maintained at the level
recommended by the Section 151 Officer.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to update the Council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy, addressing budget gaps and revenue savings amidst concerns about overspending and transparency.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
This finance monitoring report will set out
2026-27 financial position as at Month 2 and contains decisions
relating to savings and management actions.
content:
The item was introduced by Councillor
Zvikomborero Chihoro, Cabinet Member for Finance and Community
Wealth Building. The following key points were highlighted:

The report provided an early
assessment of the Council’s financial position for 2026/27,
showing a forecast General Fund overspend of just under
£11m.
The main pressures were identified
as temporary accommodation, income shortfalls and undelivered
savings within Growth and Environment, and continuing pressures in
children’s services and adult social care.
The report proposed invest-to-save
expenditure within the finance function and electric vehicle
charging, with returns to be tracked through regular
reporting.
It was noted that a fuller Quarter 1
position would be reported to Cabinet in September, including
further information on the capital programme and asset
disposals.

The Chair noted the scale of the
Council’s financial challenge, including the cost of
servicing existing debt, and stated that Cabinet Members had been
considering the financial position facing the Council.
Councillors Verity McGibbon and Diogo Costa
addressed Cabinet and raised the following points:

The improved 2025/26 year-end
position was welcomed, with thanks recorded for work in demand-led
areas including children’s social care, adult social care and
temporary accommodation.
Clarification was sought on the
pause to the Central Hill dementia service relocation, including
costs, budget provision and alternative adult social care
savings.
Questions were raised regarding
high-risk children’s services savings, including whether they
remained achievable and whether alternatives were being
considered.
Concerns were raised regarding
savings, income generation and potential reductions to library
opening hours and staffing, including the impact on residents.

Councillors Matthew Bryant and Chris Nicholson
addressed Cabinet and noted:

The proposed investment in electric
vehicle charging infrastructure was welcomed, particularly where
this would support future income generation.
Concern was raised regarding
proposed expenditure on specialist support for the Finance
Improvement Programme and the waste commissioning project, and
further detail was requested on outputs, purpose and value for
money.
It was suggested that the position
demonstrated the importance of establishing a Finance and Budget
Scrutiny Sub-Committee.
Concerns were raised regarding
decisions on libraries, asset sales and highways responsive
maintenance, and whether sufficient collaboration had taken place
in a no overall control council.

Cabinet Members made the following
comments:

The administration stated it had
inherited significant financial pressures and remained committed to
restoring financial stability.
The value of libraries was
emphasised, with alternatives to reductions being explored,
including income generation and better use of hireable spaces.
Specialist financial support and the
waste commissioning reserve were supported to help deliver robust
savings and manage major contracts effectively.
The pause to the Central Hill
dementia service relocation was defended, with concern that the
previous proposal would have left insufficient dementia day care
provision.
The need for collaboration,
transparency and a fairer local government funding settlement was
emphasised, alongside progressing electric vehicle charging at
pace.

In response to questions and comments,
officers advised that:

The allocation for specialist
financial support would be subject to a separate Cabinet Member
decision, with full transparency on the detail of any contract
award.
The support for the Finance
Improvement Programme related to technical expertise rather than
general management consultancy.
Internal staff would also be
seconded into the project team to support delivery, and progress
against the programme would be monitored.
The specialist support would assist
with improving finance processes, delivering efficiencies and
supporting savings across the programme.

In closing, the Chair stated that the
administration’s decisions would be focused on benefiting
Lambeth residents, and that the Council would seek to rebuild trust
through openness, financial transparency and collaboration. It was
noted that a forensic financial audit of spending decisions over
the previous five years had been commissioned.
RESOLVED:

To consider the forecast position
for 2026/27 of the Council’s General Fund as at the end of
May 2026.
To consider the forecast position
for 2026/27 of the Council’s Housing Revenue Account
financial position as at the end of May 2026.
To consider the management actions
already being taken by Corporate Directors to reduce the
forecast.
To consider and comment on the
progress on the delivery of in-year savings.
To note, in line with the Reserves
Strategy, which was approved by Council in March 2026, the
establishment of a £1.433m earmarked reserve by the Corporate
Director of Resources to support the Waste Commissioning
project.
To approve the use of flexible use
of capital receipts to support the development and implementation
of budget proposals up to a value of £2.5m, including an
allocation of £0.891m for support for the delivery of the
Finance Improvement Programme through a procurement compliant
framework.
To approve £2.6m, comprising
£1.3m of Section 106 funding and £1.3m of grant
funding, for a capital scheme to deliver electric vehicle charging
points, to enable additional income generation in line with agreed
savings.
To note the 2026/27 year-end
forecast as at the end of Quarter 1 would be reported to September
Cabinet.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to address a forecasted overspend in the Council's financial position for 2026/27 through various management actions and investments.

decision_maker: Corporate Director: Integrated Health and Adult Social Care
purpose:
This report seeks agreement for a waiver to
Lambeth’s Contract Standing Orders (paragraph 8.2) to enable
the direct award of a contract to Newton Consulting for the
provision of consultancy services to establish the Future of
Prevention programme in Lambeth. Newton Consulting is coordinating
this programme nationally and Lambeth Council is enrolling,
alongside other local authorities, as an early adopter. The
programme focuses on utilising predictive analytics to develop
targeted, proactive prevention approaches to improve outcomes for
older residents and reduce future demand on adult social care
services.

Direct award is proposed on the basis that Newton Consulting is
offering a specialist service tailored to a local authority context
and providing a connection to the Xantura OneView platform. The
artificial intelligence-powered platform, tested in a pilot local
authority, draws upon health and social care data to identify
people at risk of a fall ensuring preventative interventions are
targeted in the most beneficial way. There are limited competitors
for such a product and value for money from this contract is rooted
in immediate access to tested and mature predictive analytics
capability.
content:

To approve a waiver to the council’s Contract Standing Orders
(paragraph 8.2) for the direct award of a contract to Newton
Consulting for consultancy services relating to the Future of
Prevention programme, up to the value of £100,000 commencing
in April 2026.

decision_maker: Licensing Sub-Committee
content:
Presentation by the Licensing Officer
 
The
Sub-Committee was informed that this was an application for a new
premises licence for AA Plus
London - 98-100 Knights Hill West Norwood London SE27
0JL.  The applicant sought
authorisation for the following licensable activities:

 

Sale by Retail of Alcohol

Monday - Sunday                                                                                               
06:00 - 01:00

 

Opening Hours:

Monday – Sunday                                                                                              
06:00 to 01:00

 

In attendance and speaking on behalf of the
applicant, Mr Mohanraj Nagarasa
was Mr Naga Rajesh,
agent.

 

Two representations from the London Fire Brigade and
the Licensing Authority were received against the
application.  The representation from
the London Fire Brigade had been received in relation to the
submitted plans and the placement of safety equipment but had since
been withdrawn.  The other
representation from the Licensing Authority related to the timings
requested by the applicant, as they fell outside of Lambeth’s
Licensing Policy.

 

The applicant had agreed to the majority of the
proposed conditions but condition 14 (no
beers, ales, lagers or ciders of 6% ABV or above to be sold);
condition 15 (any cans or bottles of ales, beers, lagers, cider or
similar will be sold in a minimum of four); and condition 18 (the
premises shall not sell or supply miniature bottles of spirits of
50ml or less), were not agreed by the applicant.

 

The application form and proposed licensing
conditions were available from pages 15-25 of the agenda
pack.  Representations against the
application (pages 28-45 of the agenda pack) and location and
photograph of the premises (page 47 of the agenda pack).

 
The
Sub-Committee’s attention was drawn to Chapters 2, 3, 8, 9,
10 of the Statutory Guidance, and to Chapter 5, Policies 1, 10, 17
and Appendices 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 of the Statement of Licensing
Policy, as the ones particularly relevant to this
application.
 
The
options available to the Sub-Committee were set out in paragraph
5.9 of the report on page 8 of the agenda pack.

 

In response to a question from the Chair, the
Licensing Officer confirmed that the London Fire Brigade decided to
withdraw their representation upon receiving documents submitted by
the applicant regarding the premises. 
 
Presentation by the Applicant
 
Mr Naga Rajesh, informed the
Sub-Committee that:
·      
The premises was previously known as 98
Knight’s Hill and 100 Knight’s Hill which operated as
two different licensed venues. Both were managed by the applicant,
Mr Mohanraj Nagarasa and his business partner for the past two
years without any issues being reported.
·      
The two premises were licensed and able to sell
alcohol from 07:00 to 23:00 and, was considered to be a
long-standing business even before the applicant managed the
premises.
·      
During the applicant’s time in managing both
premises no complaints had been raised either from the public or
Responsible Authorities.  They were good
well-managed premises and, despite having old licences without any
conditions on those licences, appropriate measures were put forward
by the applicant to ensure that the licensing objectives were
promoted.
·      
The application would not be regarded as an extra
premises in the area and did not contribute towards the cumulative
impact as it was not in a Controlled Parking Zone (CPZ).
·      
The two premises had been merged into one premises
as they required renovation and the applicant had invested large
sums of monies into his business. 
Following a successful planning application, the restoration of the
premises had created a good look to the environment and for the
public and, a decision was made to send an application to the
Licensing Authority.
·      
The objection from the Fire Brigade had been
received due to extensive refurbishment works that had to be taken
at the premises, with new certifications being
required.  As all issues had been
resolved, the objection was withdrawn
·      
Regarding the representation raised by the Licensing
Authority about the proposed hours, whilst it was recognised that
additional hours had been requested, the premises already operated
during most of the hours proposed. 
Reducing those hours would result in the applicant being unable to
trade due to the loss of his customers. 
The applicant would ensure that the licensing objectives were
adhered to.
·      
Regarding conditions 14,15 and 18 outlined above,
which had not been agreed to, whilst the applicant appreciated that
issues existed with certain alcohol products such as strong beer,
this depended on whom such products were sold to.  Mr Mohanraj Nagarasa, applicant considered
himself to be a responsible trader and problem street drinkers were
always denied alcohol from his premises.  Only decent clientele frequented the premises to
purchase items.
·      
If conditions 14, 15 and 18 were imposed, some
customers would no longer attend the premises.  Mr Nagarasa’s trade would be affected which
would have an impact on his small business.
·      
The premises did not reside in a specialised area
for such conditions to be imposed which were regarded as blanket
conditions.  Section 182 of the
Licensing Act clearly states that conditions should not be
standardized and maybe unlawful when it cannot be demonstrated for
the appropriate and proportionate and also it should be evidenced
based.  For this premises, no direct
evidence-based information had been provided.  Whilst it was recognised that a Licensing Policy
existed, there were exceptional circumstances in this case, as a
licence already existed at the premises.
·      
Regarding the conditions, Mr Nagarasa would be happy to accept all 22 conditions
if the extra hours requested after 23:00 were granted, as this
would ensure that his clientele who frequented the premises would
be retained.
·      
In the future, if any issues later existed at the
premises, the licence could be brought to the Sub-Committee to be
reviewed.  With all the safety nets
currently in place he requested that the licence for the premises
be granted to ensure that Mr Nagarasa’s business would be
protected.
 
In response to questions from
Members, Mr Naga Rajesh, agent for the applicant,
confirmed that:
·      
The extra hours proposed was to ensure that
customers who finished work late were given the opportunity to
attend the premises and purchase both grocery and alcohol if they
wished.  If the premises remained open
without being able to sell alcohol, this would cause operational
and customer relationship issues for the applicant. 
·      
Due to the merger of both premises a large number of
household items ranging from food to cleaning products similar to a
Tesco local, existed at the premises.   Due to the massive grocery items available
the applicant would like the opportunity to sell alcohol without
undermining the licensing objectives.
·      
No off-sale products by using companies such as
Deliveroo, would operate from the premises.
·      
Issues would only result if alcohol was sold to the
wrong person and street drinkers were deterred from purchasing
alcohol to ensure that no issues resulted.
·      
Regarding condition 14, as previously mentioned
issues with superstrength lager existed but no alcohol were sold to
street drinkers by management, hence the reason for the business
being so successful. 
·      
Concerning condition 15, as late night customers
attended the store to purchase products, they would either have to
leave the premises if they did not wish to purchase four cans or
unnecessarily cause customers to purchase excessive alcohol which
could cause issues.
·      
Relating to condition 18, some good, retired
customers who were not considered to be street drinkers, normally
attended the premises to purchase small quantities of
alcohol.  If that condition was imposed,
this would result in Mr Nagarasa losing
valued customers.
·      
A refusal register was always maintained at the
premises and although Mr Rajesh
could not recall how many people were refused
alcohol for superstrength alcohol, during the past three months,
three-four refusals had been recorded.
 
Presentation by Interested Parties
 
The Licensing Officer informed
the Sub-Committee that:
·      
The Licensing Authority wished to maintain its
objection to the application on the basis that the hours sought
fell outside of the recommended terminal hour for the residential
area as set out in the Licensing Policy.  In such areas the policy licensing activities
should not be extended beyond 23:00. 
·      
The applicant had applied for a two-hour extension
beyond the policy guidance, given that the premises location was
predominantly a residential setting, an extension of alcohol sales
until 01:00 posed a significant risk that undermined the following
licensing objectives:

o  
Prevention
of public nuisance – due to the late-night activity
associated as an off licence, including noise from customers,
vehicle movement, congestion outside the premises and increased
likelihood of littering;

o  
Public
safety – associated with late night purchasing
environment.
·      
The applicant failed to demonstrate how the
extension of hours would avoid negative impact on residents, or how
the licensing objectives would be promoted when the premises
operated during the late-night hours.
·      
The Licensing Authority were also uncertain whether
any meaningful engagement with the local community had taken place
prior to the application being submitted.
·      
The Licensing Authority believed that granting the
application as submitted would have an impact on the local
community contrary to the aims of the Licensing Policy and, felt
that the application should be refused. 
If the Sub-Committee were minded in granting the application, it
was requested that the Sub-Committee consider reducing the
requested terminal hours and the opening hours being increased to
11:00 to accord with the Licensing Policy. 
·      
Regarding the conditions that were not agreed to,
condition 14 was a standard harm reduction measure applied for
off-licences situated in a residential area.  High strength beers and ciders were widely
associated with street drinking and anti-social
behaviour.  This increased the risk of
intoxication, noise disorder and vulnerability of both customers
and local residents.  Removing condition
14 increased the likelihood of late-night nuisance and disorder
but, retaining the condition, ensured that alcohol sales remained
consistent accorded with the prevention of public nuisance
objective.
·      
Condition 15 was widely implemented to discourage
single can purchasing which was strongly associated with street
drinking.  Consumption of alcohol in
public places often lead to increased litter, noise and congestion
hotspots outside the premises.  Impulse
purchasing late at night caused anti-social behaviour in
residential areas.  Removing that
condition made it easier for individuals to purchase single items
for immediate consumption outside the premises which undermined
both the public safety and prevention of public nuisance
objectives.
·      
Miniatures (condition 18) were frequently linked to
problematic drinking patterns because they were cheap, easy to
conceal and designed for immediate consumption.  Miniatures tended to be consumed repeatedly and
rapidly on the streets and in the neighbourhood nearby residential
areas that contributed to anti-social behaviour.  Individuals often purchased miniatures who sought
quick intoxication rather than planned responsible consumption,
which resulted in high levels of litter, as empty miniatures were
commonly discarded in public spaces in residential areas,
particularly where long trading hours were proposed.  The sale of miniatures also increased the
likelihood of disruptive behaviour, anti-social behaviour and
alcohol related nuisance in immediate vicinities.
 
In response to questions from
Members, the Licensing Officer confirmed
that:
·      
Conditions 14, 15 and 18 were not applied to all
licensed premises.
 
The
Chair invited Mr Naga Rajesh, agent for the
applicant, back to address the Sub-Committee to answer
additional questions, and he confirmed:
·      
Mr Nagarasa had managed
the premises for the up to four years without any
issues.
·      
If the application was not granted Mr
Nagarasa’s business would be affected due to the loss of his
clientele. 
·      
A refusal register was available at the premises for
inspection.
·      
Although a new application had been submitted, the
premises already existed in the area, and this should be regarded
as exceptional circumstances.
·      
Planning permission had been agreed for the
applicant to be able to trade for 24-hours and whilst this fell
outside of the Licensing Act, no evidence existed to demonstrate
that there were any issues associated with the premises.
·      
The customers that frequented the premises were
regarded as regular local residents, with some attending when they
left work.  The applicant would ensure
that the premises continued to be well managed to prevent the
proposed hours having to be reduced.
 
Adjournment and Decision
 
At 07.43 pm, the Sub-Committee
withdrew from the meeting together with the legal advisor and clerk
to deliberate in private.
 
The Sub-Committee had heard and
considered representations from The Licensing Officer, and
Mr Naga Rajesh, agent for the
applicant, Mr Mohanraj
Nagarasa.
 
Legal advice was given to the
Sub-Committee on the options open to them and the need for any
decision to be proportionate. The Sub-Committee decided to refuse
the application for the following reasons:
 
·      
The Sub-Committee considered an application for a
premises licence which was a new application for the sale and
retail of alcohol for AA Plus London, 98-100 Knights Hill, London
SE27 0JL.
 
·      
The Sub-Committee determined to grant the
application and agreed that the following terms would promote the
licensing objectives:
 

o  
The sale of
retail and alcohol Monday-Sunday 06:00-01:00 and opening hours from
Monday-Sunday 06:00-01:00.

o  
The proposed
conditions contained on pages 23-25 of the agenda pack and also
referred to on pages 28-30 of the agenda pack be attached to the
licence except for the proposed condition 15 (any cans or bottles
of ales, beers, lagers, cider or similar will be sold in a minimum
of four). Conditions 14 (no beers, ales, lagers or ciders of 6% ABV or above to be sold);
and condition 18 (the premises shall not sell or supply miniature
bottles of spirits of 50ml or less) must be included on the
licence.
 
RESOLVED: To grant the
application.
 
Announcement of Decision
 
Members returned to the meeting
and the Chair informed those present of the decision to grant the
application and provided reasons for the decision as outlined
above. The Chair confirmed that written notification of the
decision would be sent in due course.
topline: The Licensing Sub-Committee has decided to grant a new premises licence for AA Plus London, allowing the sale of alcohol from 06:00 to 01:00 daily.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
To report progress on the New Homes Programme
and establish the programme for 2026/27.
content:
The item was introduced by Councillor Danial
Adilypour, Deputy Leader of the Council (Housing, Investment and
New Homes). The following was highlighted:

The significant scale of housing
need in Lambeth, with over 28,000 households on the waiting list
and 4,400 in temporary accommodation, and that delivering genuinely
affordable housing remained a key priority.
The progress made over the past year
was outlined, including completion of the Fenwick Place scheme
(100% social rent), planning approval for Somerleyton Road (56% affordable housing), and
establishing the New Homes Hexagon partnership to deliver over 500
homes.
The administration’s focus on
delivering new homes for residents was emphasised, including recent
completions such as Billy Cox House, which would provide new social
housing for local families.

Councillor Scott Ainslie, Green Group Leader,
addressed Cabinet and noted:

Concerns regarding delays and lack
of progress across multiple housing sites, including long-standing
schemes remaining undeveloped or delayed in the planning process,
and questioned the consistency and credibility of delivery
timelines and reporting.
Concerns that national and regional
policy changes could reduce affordable housing requirements and
queried the risk of schemes in the pipeline being revised down
following viability assessments, noting this had not been addressed
in the report.

Georgina Schueller also addressed Cabinet and
raised the following points:

Concerns that the proposed rent
increase would primarily cover rising costs, with limited impact on
improving repairs, and highlighted high expenditure on disrepair
litigation.
Queried whether reliance on
efficiencies would be sufficient to maintain housing standards
without increasing long-term costs.
Raised concerns regarding the use of
housing stock, including the refurbishment of former leaseholder
properties and use of demolition estates for temporary
accommodation.
Questioned the Council’s
definition of affordability and the transparency of housing data,
including the omission of demolition figures, and whether proposed
homes would be genuinely affordable to those on the housing waiting
list.

 
Cabinet Members made the following
comments:

It was stated that despite national
policy changes, the Council remained committed to maximising
affordable housing delivery, highlighting success at Somerleyton Road achieved through a competitive
procurement process, with the intention to continue exceeding
minimum requirements.
A concern was raised regarding
inaccurate public claims that only four council homes had been
delivered in recent years, and officers confirmed that Appendix 1
accurately recorded 359 social rent homes delivered since
2017.
It was highlighted that recent
developments in Brixton had delivered approximately 55 social rent
homes, supporting families from temporary accommodation and the
housing waiting list.
It was highlighted that Right to Buy
receipts were being maximised, including investment of £3.5m
to buy back properties, supporting residents in housing need and
making best use of limited resources.
It was noted, following
consideration at the Equity and Justice Panel, that the New Homes
Programme would support addressing housing inequalities,
particularly for households in temporary accommodation and those on
the housing register.
The Panel welcomed the equalities
impact assessment (EQIA), highlighting its balanced approach to
long-term benefits and short-term impacts, alongside commitments to
resident engagement, inclusive design and ongoing monitoring to
ensure equitable outcomes.

In response to questions and comments,
officers stated that:

The housing pipeline included both
confirmed and indicative sites, which was standard practice to
support funding bids.
Recent engagement with the Greater
London Authority (GLA) had supported development of this approach
to secure long-term funding and future delivery.
The Council was working with
partners to identify additional housing sites, including developing
around 40 sites for a funding bid, and continued to explore further
opportunities and new approaches to increase housing supply.
Strong market engagement and a
procurement strategy with robust viability testing and contractual
requirements had supported delivery of affordable housing,
including Somerleyton Road.
The schemes would generate
employment and training opportunities, citing Somerleyton Road where 716 construction jobs and 37
apprenticeships had been created, and confirmed that local residents were actively involved in
procurement, planning and co-design processes.
Officers advised that environmental
sustainability and achieving net zero carbon were embedded from the
outset of all developments, with schemes assessed on whole-life
carbon impacts and subject to ongoing evaluation to support
continuous improvement.
It was highlighted that schemes such
as Fenwick Place and Somerleyton Road
demonstrated strong environmental performance, including reduced
construction waste and enhanced energy efficiency through measures
such as renewable technologies and exceeding planning targets.
Engagement with Brixton Street Gym
had identified a preferred alternative site, with a commitment to
secure a temporary solution.
The Council had shifted to a
partnership delivery model since 2022, working with developers to
share risk, with robust procurement, financial and viability checks
in place throughout to ensure delivery.

In closing, the Councillor Adilypour
reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to delivering 10,000 new
homes over the next decade, with 40% affordable housing, and
emphasised the administration’s clear focus on tackling the
housing crisis and delivering homes for residents.
RESOLVED:

To approve the projects and
workstreams for the New Homes Programme (NHP) in 2026/27 and the
continuation of deliverables progressed in 2025/26, and to delegate
authority to advance these projects to the Corporate Director of
Housing in consultation with the Deputy Leader of the Council
(Housing, Investment and New Homes).

 

To note the council’s ambition
to enable the delivery of at least 10,000 new homes in Lambeth over

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
The Quarter 3 2025/26 Budget Monitoring Report
will set out the Council’s latest forecast year end position
for revenue and capital expenditure and income, including
management actions being taken, financial performance information
including income collection, debt recovery, treasury management and
reserves. The report will contain decisions relating to capital and
revenue expenditure, savings and income that will address the
council’s financial position both in year and for future
years.
content:
The item was introduced by Councillor Judith
Cavanagh, Cabinet Member for Finance (Acting). The following key
points were highlighted:

The Council continued to face
significant financial pressures driven by demand in statutory
services and the long-term impact of underfunding.
It was noted that while many
councils were seeking Government support, Lambeth’s
Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) application was primarily to
rebuild reserves from previous years, with only a small element to
balance the next year’s budget with no anticipated ongoing
reliance on EFS.
The scale of the application
reflected significant recent spending on temporary accommodation,
which had depleted reserves, and that Government support would
replenish reserves and strengthen financial stability.
Action was underway to stabilise
social care and temporary accommodation costs, alongside wider
efficiencies and management reductions; progress had been
recognised by external auditors and inspection outcomes, with
thanks recorded to officers.

Councillors Scott Ainslie, Green Group Leader,
and Matthew Bryant, Liberal Democrats Deputy Group Leader,
addressed the meeting and stated:

An £11.1m gap had emerged in
Table 14 (Savings Delivery Forecast) between November and the
current Quarter 3 report, echoing external auditors’ concerns
regarding savings delivery.
£30m of Target Operating Model
savings had been introduced late in the previous budget process
with limited clarity, and only £0.5m of the £15.37m
expected this year had been delivered, raising concerns about
financial grip and oversight.
The Council’s reliance on
Oracle for its accountancy system was questioned, alongside issues
relating to income collection and delays in Community
Infrastructure Levy (CIL) receipts.

During discussion, Councillor Rezina Chowdhury
highlighted an error in the appendix regarding savings delivery,
clarifying that the lighting technology programme had been
withdrawn from the savings proposal, not paused, she advised that
when considering the proposal she concluded as  Cabinet Member  that
cost and effectiveness did not justify progression, particularly in
light of safety considerations; concern was expressed about
misinformation circulated publicly. Officers confirmed the wording
would be corrected and assured Cabinet that the scheme did not
appear in the forthcoming capital programme, with the reference
having remained in error from the previous quarter prior to the
review concluding.
Following comments and questions, officers
made clarifications:

It was advised that savings were
monitored monthly, and although some had slipped into future years,
this was offset by improved forecasts in key areas such as
temporary accommodation, adult social care and reduced borrowing
and interest costs.
Officers clarified that a red rating
did not necessarily indicate that a saving was undeliverable, but
in some cases reflected re-profiling where delivery had slipped
beyond the original timescale.
Target Operating Model savings had
been superseded by agreed proposals in the November and February
budget reports and, although not delivered in-year, were expected
to be achieved in future years and were not considered at
risk.
Housing policy and operational
changes were delivering a sustained reduction in temporary
accommodation costs, with confidence that the service would operate
within budget next year and lessen reliance on reserves.

Cabinet Members raised the following
points:

The Oracle system was critical to
core functions including finance, HR and data management, and no
viable alternative had been presented that offered comparable value
or continuity.
Temporary accommodation was not a
sustainable long-term solution, and the Council’s focus
remained on moving families into secure homes, alongside
strengthened demand management and right-sizing in social care to
deliver savings; independent reviewers had encouraged further
invest-to-save measures.
Red ratings reflected transparent
reporting and did not necessarily indicate failure, as many savings
were in progress and expected to be delivered later in the
year.
Overspends within Children, Families
and Education, particularly special educational needs and
disability (SEND) transport, were largely driven by national
structural underfunding, with Government proposals anticipated to
address High Needs Block pressures.
Thanks were recorded to the
children’s social care team for reducing agency reliance and
strengthening workforce stability.

RESOLVED:
 

1.   
To consider the forecast position for 2025-26 of the
Council’s General Fund as at the end of December 2025.

2.   
To consider the forecast position for 2025-26 of the
Council’s Housing Revenue Account financial position as at
the end of December 2025.

3.   
To approve the proposal to optimise support provided for Home to
School Transport assistance to reduce costs from 2026-27.

4.   
To consider the management actions already being taken by Corporate
Directors to reduce the forecast position to within budget by the
end of the financial year.

5.   
To consider and comment on the progress on the delivery of in-year
savings.

6.   
To note the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise
future borrowing and associated revenue costs.

7.   
To note the 2025-26 Outturn report will be reported to July
Cabinet.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to address significant financial pressures and approve proposals to optimize support for Home to School Transport assistance.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
To agree the 2026/27 General Fund Budget to be
recommended to Council. The Revenue and Capital Budget report will
set out the General Fund budget for 2026-27 and planning totals for
the following four years together with a refreshed Medium Term
Financial Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy, Capital
Programme, Fees & Charges and Council Tax setting.
content:
The item was introduced by Councillor Judith
Cavanagh, Cabinet Member for Finance (Acting). The following key
points were highlighted:

The report set out the proposed
Revenue and Capital Budget for 2026/27 and the Medium-Term
Financial Strategy (MTFS) to 2029/30.
Councils had faced sustained
real-terms funding reductions since 2010 despite rising demand,
creating a challenging legacy, with the current Government
demonstrating a commitment to reform.
The Budget would prioritise the
delivery of high-quality public services identified as important to
residents, including support for vulnerable children, protection of
street cleaning services, and continued investment in
London-leading services supporting women and girls who had survived
domestic abuse and violence.
The Budget included an updated
Capital Strategy focused on long-term sustainability and reducing
debt servicing costs to support delivery of Borough Plan priorities
and ambitions.
As part of this approach, the
Council would seek to reduce slippage in capital programme
delivery, maximise the use of grant funding and alternative
financing sources, and apply capital receipts to reduce
borrowing.
The Council remained committed to
openness, honesty and transparency, guided by its values to protect
the most vulnerable wherever possible and maintain clear dialogue
with residents.

Councillors Scott Ainslie and Matthew Bryant
also addressed Cabinet and noted:

Clarification was sought on the
funding of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), particularly the
balance between capital receipts and short-term borrowing, and a
consolidated table of previously approved savings (£99m,
£83m and £130m) was requested to show overlaps and
cumulative impact.
The Council was urged to maximise
asset value, referencing past investment in affordable workspace at
Phoenix House and International House, and to prioritise economic
growth and conclude the capital review.
Concern was expressed that reducing
maximum council tax support to 73.5% would disproportionately
impact vulnerable residents.
Further clarification was requested
on how much of the EFS would be financed through asset sales,
including the status of surplus assets and capital receipts.
Disappointment was expressed that
the electric vehicle infrastructure scheme was not firmly included
in the forthcoming capital programme, despite the previous decision
to bring the service in-house.

In response to questions and comments,
officers advised that:

The £116m EFS application was
confirmed, with the long-term intention to fund it through capital
receipts; however, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy prudently
assumed interim borrowing, with earlier asset sales reducing
borrowing and improving the budget position.
As set out in the Capital Strategy
and Asset Management Framework, work was underway across finance
and property teams to identify assets for disposal, with updates on
capital receipts and borrowing levels to be reported during the
forthcoming financial year.
Internal borrowing, using available
cash balances to fund capital investment, was standard treasury
management practice and more flexible and cost-effective than
external borrowing, as it avoided higher interest costs.

Prior to the agreement of recommendations,
officers noted that recommendation 20 had been omitted from the
final published report in error, and that it should be inserted to
read: “To approve the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy
as set out at Appendix 13.”
In closing, the Cabinet Member for Finance
stated that the Budget prioritised early intervention and
prevention, including moving families into permanent homes,
supporting vulnerable children and adults, protecting women and
girls, and creating opportunities for young people, and expressed
pride in a Budget focused on improving outcomes despite significant
challenges ahead.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
Lambeth has recently been re-accredited as a
Borough of Sanctuary by the City of Sanctuary organisation from
2025 – 2028. As part of this process, Lambeth had to produce
a new strategy which sets out our vision to improve access to
support for all people seeking sanctuary and amplify the voices of
those with lived experience.

To finalise the strategy, Cabinet is asked to approve and adopt it
and to also note the successful reaccreditation of Lambeth as a
Borough of Sanctuary.
content:
The item was introduced by Councillor Nanda
Manley-Browne, Cabinet Member for Healthier Communities (job
share). The following key points were highlighted:

Lambeth had a long-standing
commitment to being a Borough of Sanctuary, rooted in the Borough
Plan commitment to equity and justice.
The Council was awarded Borough of
Sanctuary status in December 2022 and had successfully achieved
reaccreditation in December 2025, with the refreshed Strategy
representing the final stage of that process.
The Strategy had been shaped through
engagement with the Lambeth Sanctuary Forum, voluntary and
community sector partners, and people with lived experience of
seeking sanctuary.
The accompanying action plan set out
measurable actions, including translated housing information,
skills programmes, safeguarding measures and strengthened referral
pathways.

Cabinet Members made the following
contributions:

International classes in schools
were highlighted as a strong example of practical support,
providing intensive English language support and structured
introduction to the UK education system.
It was stated that the Strategy
provided an opportunity for the Council to reaffirm its values,
demonstrate that Lambeth stood firmly against hate and division,
and confirm its commitment to supporting those most in need.
It was emphasised that while the
Council’s support was crucial, partnership working with
voluntary and community organisations was equally important in
supporting skill development and enabling people seeking sanctuary
to embed themselves successfully within the community.

In response to questions and comments,
officers advised that the action plan had been developed through
multi-agency consultation and engagement.
RESOLVED:

1.   
To approve and adopt the Lambeth Borough of Sanctuary Strategy for
delivery between 2025- 2028 (Appendix A).

2.   
To note the successful reaccreditation of Lambeth as a Borough of
Sanctuary by City of Sanctuary UK.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and adopt the Lambeth Borough of Sanctuary Strategy for delivery between 2025-2028.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
Lambeth has declared all of the borough as an
Air Quality Management Area for the pollutants nitrogen dioxide and
particulate matter. The new Air Quality Action Plan has been
produced as part of our duty to London Local Air Quality
Management. The plan outlines the action we will take to improve
air quality in Lambeth from 2026 to 2028 .This action plan replaces
the previous action plan which ran from 2023 to 2025.
content:
The item was
introduced by Councillor Rezina Chowdhury, Deputy Leader of the
Council (Sustainable Lambeth and Clean Air). The following key
points were highlighted:

Clean air was
fundamental to delivering a healthy, fair, and thriving borough and
was central to the Borough Plan commitment to building a healthier,
safer and more equitable Lambeth by 2030.
Air pollution
disproportionately affected children, older people, residents with
heart and lung conditions, multi-ethnic communities and those in
more deprived neighbourhoods; tackling these inequalities
underpinned the Borough Plan and the Council’s approach to
transport and climate action.
The Action Plan
built on previous success and set out seven priority areas,
including cleaner transport and freight, reducing emissions from
buildings and construction, and strengthening monitoring,
enforcement and public awareness.
Lambeth remained on
track to meet its borough-wide Air Quality Vision targets by 2030,
including alignment with World Health Organisation guidelines.

Zak Bond, Clean
Cities, addressed the meeting and highlighted:

Lambeth’s
leadership in expanding electric vehicle (EV) charging
infrastructure and its ambition for a car club on every street and
estate by 2030.
The significant
contribution of diesel vans to oxides of Nitrogen (Nox) and PM2.5
emissions.
The potential for
electric-only loading bays, increased support for cargo bike
adoption and exploration of zero-emission freight zones in
partnership with neighbouring boroughs.

Claire McDonald,
Solve the School Run, addressed the meeting and highlighted:

Travel for London
(TfL) evidence showing School Streets reduced nitrogen dioxide by
23% and achieved an 18% modal shift.
The long-term
behavioural impact of sustained School Street schemes.
That 12 eligible
primary schools were still awaiting School Street implementation,
affecting approximately 5,000 children.
The importance of
extending School Streets to secondary schools.

Ben Pearce, Impact
on Urban Health, addressed the meeting and highlighted:

The importance of
measurable targets aligned with World Health Organisation
guidelines.
The need to centre
equity more explicitly within the Action Plan.
The importance of
ensuring that feedback from the Air Quality Forum influenced policy
decisions.
Continued
collaboration on construction emissions and evaluation of the
Construction Compliance Officer role.

In response to
questions and comments, officers advised that:

An Equality Impact
Assessment had been undertaken on the Action Plan, which concluded
that it would deliver net positive impacts for children, older
people, residents with existing health conditions and Black and
minority communities, with no significant adverse impacts
identified.
Trials to
incentivise electric cargo bikes for businesses were already
underway, including in Waterloo and the South Bank, and lessons
learned would be used to inform potential wider rollout,
recognising the role cargo bikes could play in supporting
businesses to transition to cleaner freight and service delivery
models.
Equity was central
to the Air Quality Action Plan, with the Air Quality Forum
established to ensure those most affected by poor air quality
shaped priorities and informed future iterations of the Plan.
Lambeth was leading
construction emissions work with Impact on Urban Health and
Southwark, with the Construction Compliance Officer role intended
to continue beyond the current funding period and learning embedded
across planning and regulatory services.
Officers were
working closely with the procurement team to ensure that any key
performance indicators (KPIs) introduced within contracts were
realistic and deliverable, recognising the importance of
procurement in reducing emissions, particularly across the
Council’s fleet.
Officers were
working with Public Health to align air quality and respiratory
health priorities, including promoting the Asthma Friendly Schools
programme to support vulnerable children and young people.


 

RESOLVED:
1. To adopt the
Lambeth Air Quality Action Plan 2026-2028.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt the Lambeth Air Quality Action Plan 2026-2028.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
Each year local authorities must set rents for
the forthcoming financial year and provide each tenant with
statutory notice of any proposed rent and service charge
changes.

The report sets out the proposals for the Housing Revenue Account
(HRA) rents and tenants’ service charges for the 2026/27
financial year, which will inform the HRA budget and Business Plan
to be approved by Cabinet in February.
content:
The item was
introduced by Councillor Danial Adilypour, Deputy Leader of the
Council (Housing, Investment and New Homes). The following key
points were highlighted:

The report set out
proposed rent and service charge levels for 2026/27 in line with
the national rent policy framework.
The proposals
balanced the need to maintain investment in housing stock,
including repairs, damp and mould remediation and building safety,
with affordability considerations for tenants.
The financial
implications for the Housing Revenue Account Business Plan were
outlined.

Georgina Schueller
addressed Cabinet and:

Raised concerns
about the proposed 4.8% rent increase and additional rent
convergence and service charge increases, warning of the impact on
tenants, particularly those just above the benefits threshold.
Noted that greater
priority should be given to investing rent income in repairs and
tackling the root causes of disrepair rather than litigation.
Expressed concern
about rising arrears and homelessness and urged the Council to
improve housing management and lobby government on historic Housing
Revenue Account (HRA) funding and debt issues.

Councillor Matthew
Bryant addressed Cabinet and queried why the Rent Setting Question
and Answer (Q&A) session with tenants did not take place prior
to Cabinet. The Member stated that while there was no statutory
requirement to consult, it would have been preferable for Cabinet
to hear tenants’ views before setting rents.
In response to
comments and questions, officers noted that:

The Q&A session
had been delayed due to uncertainty around rent convergence
guidance, which had only recently been confirmed, to ensure
residents received clear and complete information.
Officers advised
that due to changes in Universal Credit data sharing, the Council
no longer held detailed benefit information, and while around 60%
were estimated to receive support, this could not be confirmed as
the data was held by the Department for Work and Pensions
(DWP).
HRA borrowing was
used to fund the wider capital programme and was reinvested
directly into the Council’s housing stock, ensuring that
borrowing supported improvements to the homes and estates in which
Lambeth tenants lived.
Officers advised
that each £1 per week rent convergence increase equated to
approximately £1.2m of annual HRA income, and that delays to
convergence had contributed to a shortfall of around £6 per
week per property, limiting investment capacity.


RESOLVED:

1.   
To approve the increase in rent by CPI+1% (4.8%), this being the
maximum rent increase possible according to the Regulator of Social
Housing for continuing tenancies with effect from 6 April 2026.

2.   
 To approve convergence to formula rent
at the maximum rate that is determined by HM Government.

3.   
To approve the approach to setting tenant and leasehold service
charges as set out in 2.12 – 2.18, and agree the changes
proposed in Appendix 1, with effect from 6 April 2026.

4.   
To approve the increases in sheltered housing management service
charge as set out in paragraph 2.16 and 2.17, and Appendix 1, with
effect from 6 April 2026.

5.   
To approve the increase in charges for garage rental, and no change
in sheds and cycle storage rental, as set out in Appendix 2 with
effect from 6 April 2026.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve rent and service charge increases for 2026/27, despite concerns raised about the impact on tenants and the need for greater investment in repairs.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
Approval of our Children and Young
People’s Placement Sufficiency Strategy
content:
The item was taken
as the second substantive item and was introduced by Councillor Ben
Kind, Cabinet Member for Children, Young People and Families. The
following key points were highlighted:

The Strategy set
out the Council’s approach to ensuring sufficient,
high-quality placements for children in care and care experienced
young people over the period 2025–2030.
Lambeth had
recruited 24 new foster carers in the previous year, the highest
number in London, reflecting significant improvement and the
strength of the Council’s holistic “One Lambeth”
support offer for carers and young people.
The approach
aligned with Child Friendly Lambeth principles and strengthened the
Council’s corporate parenting responsibilities.

Councillor Matthew
Bryant, Liberal Democrats Deputy Group Leader, emphasised the
importance of the Edge of Care approach in reducing entries to
care, noting that numbers had stabilised at just under 400, and
asked what reduction was anticipated and whether targets had been
set; he also queried planned foster carer recruitment initiatives
and lessons learned from the previous year’s success.
In response to
questions and comments, officers advised that:

Recruitment
processes had been redesigned to improve responsiveness and
candidate experience, including faster enquiry responses,
streamlined assessments, prioritised medical checks and more
proactive, visible community-based recruitment activity.
A multi-faceted
strategy had been implemented to attract carers, alongside
strengthened support and retention arrangements to ensure foster
carers remained with the Council.
Edge of Care work
was being strengthened through the Families First Partnership to
improve integrated early help; further analysis was underway to
quantify impact and early permanence outcomes, with more detailed
figures to follow.
Improved analysis
of projected need and the profile of children entering care enabled
more targeted foster carer recruitment, including engagement with
faith communities and specific neighbourhoods, ensuring campaigns
reflected the diversity and characteristics of children in
care.
It was noted that
under the Council’s Housing Allocation Policy, prospective
and approved foster carers were placed in the highest priority
banding for accommodation, reflecting the Council’s
commitment to supporting fostering wherever possible.

Councillor Ben Kind

Cabinet recorded its

Experienced Young People 2025-30 Strategy.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
The December Financial Planning and Medium
Term Strategy Report will provide an update on the economic
outlook, pressures, risk areas and set out the revenue funding
deficit for 2025-30 together with proposals to close the funding
gap
content:
The item was
introduced by Councillor Judith Cavanagh, Acting Cabinet Member for
Finance. The following key points were highlighted:

The report set out
the Council’s Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
2025–2030 against a backdrop of significant financial
pressures, including rising temporary accommodation costs,
increasing social care demand and borrowing pressures.
The Strategy
outlined savings proposals, transformation activity and
strengthened financial governance arrangements.
The approach aimed
to stabilise the Council’s financial position while
protecting priority services where possible.

The Corporate
Director of Resources, Zena Cooke, noted that the final Local
Government Finance Settlement had been delayed until the following
week, which would impact recommendation three by moving the
timetable back by one week.
Councillor Matthew
Bryant addressed Cabinet and noted:

That eight
recommendations had been made by Scrutiny, including a request that
savings and spending proposals presented to Budget Council provide
greater clarity and detail.
There were three
specific savings proposals where further detail was sought: item 71
(Sustainable Adult Social Care), given demand-led pressures in the
service; item 58 (Parks Restructuring), including the overall parks
budget context; and item 56 (Vale Street Depot), seeking
clarification on alternative funding models under consideration and
whether these could involve additional charges.

In response to
questions and comments, officers advised that:

Further details on
the size of the Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) application
would be set out in the budget report due for publication on 13
February.
The application
comprised three elements: rebuilding depleted reserves to improve
financial resilience; balancing the budget in the short term to
allow time to deliver necessary transformation; and addressing
specific one-off pressures previously identified.
In relation to the
Sustainable Adult Social Care savings, officers advised that the
proposal focused on delivering more cost-effective care packages
through enhanced data analysis, regular reassessment, and improved
commissioning across client groups, equating to approximately 3.5%
over four years and was considered deliverable.
A further element
of around £0.5m related to the expanded use of the Sanctuary
Grant to support services beyond adult social care.
It was confirmed
that the proposed parks restructuring would protect frontline
service delivery, prioritising visible on-the-ground staff
presence, routine maintenance, inspections and health and safety
functions.
In relation to the
Vale Street Depot, officers advised that discussions were ongoing
with the Western Riverside Waste Authority (WRWA) and it was too
early to provide detailed options.
Members were
assured that proposals would be developed closely with the Deputy
Leader and would avoid adverse impacts on residents.
Officers advised
that while total reserves at the end of 2024/25 stood at
£55.7m, general fund balances and unallocated reserves were
only £5m, significantly below the Section 151 Officer’s
recommended level of around 10% of net revenue budget
(approximately £45m).
It was noted that a
substantial proportion of reserves were ring-fenced, including
capital reserves such as the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL)
and joint reserves held with health partners, and were therefore
not available to address demand pressures or support general
revenue expenditure.
A detailed review
of reserves had confirmed that usable balances were limited, and
EFS was therefore being sought in part to rebuild reserves and
improve financial resilience.

 

RESOLVED:

To agree and
approve proposed savings summarised in Table 1 and detailed in
Appendix 1. 2.
To note that
savings proposals in Appendix 1 were considered by the Equity and
Justice (E&J) Panel on 22 January 2026, and that a verbal
update will be given to Cabinet at the meeting.
To note that the
Final Local Government Finance Settlement (FLGFS) is expected to be
published week commencing 9 February 2026. Assumptions currently
included in the MTFS will be updated as necessary following
analysis of any impact from the FLGFS.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve proposed savings to address significant financial pressures and stabilize the Council's financial position.

intent to make an order (the “Order”) under section

267582-00-T-SU-003 Rev E (appendix B) and 267582-00-T-SU-005 Rev C
